summary: Redwood ran an edge-cases focused demo for NexGen: long-context handling, high TPS load, streaming backpressure, and timeouts. NexGen is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment; main concerns were p99 latency, KV cache effectiveness for long contexts, streaming resiliency under backpressure, and audit/KMS for compliance. Agreed to run a 48-hour benchmark and share configs, pricing, and security docs. Next deep dive scheduled for early Jan to discuss VPC/on-prem networking.
transcript:
[00:00] Alice (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we know it's Friday so we'll aim to keep this tight. I'm Alice from Redwood, joined by Ben from our SE team and Lina from product. Can everyone hear me okay?
[00:09] Marco (NexGen): Yeah loud and clear. Thanks Alice.
[00:12] Priya (NexGen): Yep all good. We are excited — we put together some fairly gnarly workloads we want to walk through.
[00:21] Ben (Redwood SE): Great, high level agenda — we'll quickly show Console and API flows, then hit three edge cases: long context handling (KV cache behavior), high TPS sustained load, and streaming backpressure/timeouts. We'll call out tradeoffs and recommended configs.
[00:36] Jonas (NexGen): Quick ask — when you say long context, does that mean multi-document threads or like 200k token inputs?
[00:45] Ben (Redwood SE): Good question. For today we'll demo ~100k token synthetic context across multiple docs and show how prefix caching avoids re-encoding. We won't actually push 200k in the demo, but we can discuss headroom and quantization impacts.
[00:58] Speaker 1: (background) okay yep
[01:02] Alice: I'll share my screen — starting with Console, here's the route that NeXGen might use for chat ingestion, you can see per-route batching window, caching toggles, and model variants.
[01:20] Priya: The UI looks familiar — can you show where KV cache TTLs are configurable? We plan to keep customer sessions for up to 24 hours in memory.
[01:28] Ben: Sure — under 'Optimize' you can set prefix caching, kv-cache retention, and warming policies. Note: retention in-memory has cost/eviction tradeoffs; for very long sessions we recommend a hybrid cache: in-memory for hot sessions, backing store for cold.
[01:45] Marco: Cold store... are you talking about Redis or Redwood-managed blobstore?
[01:50] Ben: Both are possible. For Dedicated or Private, customers usually run Redis in the VPC, we expose a cache API so the runtime can hydrate on demand. For Hosted we can provide managed cold-store with encryption at rest. There might be small extra egress if you hydrate from an external store.
[02:06] Priya: How do you avoid re-encoding large histories? We get killed on CPU costs when we re-encode.
[02:13] Ben: That's where our persistent KV cache and prefix sharing helps: tokens after the last attention window are stored as KV, when you append new user messages the runtime only encodes the new tokens and stitches with cached KV. It avoids full re-encode for long contexts. The caveat — different model variants or quantization changes can invalidate caches.
[02:32] Priya: So when we do model rollouts, do we lose cache warmth?
[02:36] Ben: Potentially, yes. We support rolling cache warmers and can do blue/green model swaps with cache prewarm to reduce cold starts. It's an ops effort but we've done it with customers.
[02:45] Marco: Ok, move to TPS. Our target is sustained 2k requests/sec with occasional spikes to 5k for short bursts. p99 should be under 350ms.
[02:58] Ben: That's helpful. For text generation with 2k RPS we look at batching efficiency and whether you use streaming. If you stream token-by-token to clients, CPU and GPU utilization patterns change — batching helps GPU efficiency but increases tail latency.
[03:15] Priya: We need low p99 more than absolute throughput for some endpoints. Can you show the autoscaling options for Dedicated?
[03:23] Alice: On Dedicated you can set target p95/p99 SLOs, and autoscaler adjusts replica count and queue depth. We also offer burst capacity for short spikes. For Hosted, we have multi-tenant pools and prioritization tiers.
[03:36] Jonas: In past tests with other vendors, backpressure on streaming endpoints caused client-side timeouts even though server kept generating. How does Redwood handle streaming backpressure?
[03:47] Ben: Good point. Our streaming system supports built-in circuit-breaking and backpressure-aware batching. If the client can't keep up, the runtime can switch to chunked responses or a fully-buffered response depending on policy. There's also a per-connection send window and we emit metrics so you can detect slow consumers.
[04:05] Priya: What happens to GPU memory if a lot of clients are slow and accumulate generated tokens on the server?
[04:12] Ben: We avoid keeping generated tokens in GPU memory — the runtime flushes to local buffer and then to network. There is a buffer memory footprint on the host. We enforce per-connection caps and can drop or truncate long outputs if necessary. These are configurable policies tied to SLOs.
[04:30] Speaker 1: (mumbles) what about timeouts?
[04:33] Ben: There are two timeout layers: network/streaming timeouts and inference timeouts. For inference timeouts we have per-request CPU/GPU wall limits and we return partial results + an explicit timeout error code if we hit it; you can set retry/backoff in the SDK.
[04:49] Marco: Can you demo a scenario where streaming client is slow and triggers backpressure, so we see the behavior?
[04:55] Ben: Yep — switching to a simulated load in Console. I'm going to start a 500 concurrent clients, but make 20% of them slow by artificially delaying reads.
[05:06] [05:06] Ben shares load generator — starting run
[05:10] [05:10] Ben: You can see metrics — queue depth rises for slow consumers, backpressure flags trigger, and the runtime changes to chunked streaming for affected sessions. Notice the spike in server-side buffer allocation but not GPU OOMs.
[05:24] Priya: Hmm looks okay. What about end-to-end latency for the fast clients while you've got slow ones?
[05:30] Ben: The config here prioritizes p99 for fast clients — slow clients are chunked and deprioritized. p50/p95 remain stable, p99 moves a bit but within target.
[05:39] Jonas: In a multi-tenant hosted pool, could noisy neighbors cause similar issues?
[05:44] Ben: On Hosted we mitigate with per-tenant quotas and soft isolation; for strict isolation use Dedicated. We also have workload-aware routing that can redirect heavy traffic to cheaper model variants to preserve SLOs.
[05:58] Marco: About timeouts — we've seen earlier integrations where long-running generations hit network proxies and the proxy kills the stream after 30s. Any guidance?
[06:07] Alice: We recommend end-to-end timeout alignment: LB, gateway, client library, and SDK defaults. Redwood SDKs expose keepalives and chunk-level progress, so even if a proxy times out, you can retry/resume in some cases. For critical flows we suggest private deployment so you can control proxies.
[06:25] Priya: Ok, show us API example for streaming with retry semantics.
[06:29] Ben: (shares code) here's a snippet: start stream with resume token, set per-chunk ack, fallback to batched response on repeated backpressure. Also here's a link to the runbook: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/streaming-backpressure-runbook.
[06:46] Speaker 1: (background) runbook noted
[06:49] Marco: Security questions — we are SOC2 required and need customer-managed keys and audit logs.
[06:55] Ben: We support KMS/HSM integrations, full audit logs with per-request metadata, and SSO via SAML/Okta. For Private, keys stay in your KMS and we never see plaintext. For Hosted, we offer BYOK options with HSM-backed key wrapping.
[07:10] Priya: Does telemetry include full prompts? That's a compliance concern.
[07:13] Ben: By default we store hashed/metadata, but you can configure scrubbing and redaction. For Private deployments, telemetry can be turned off entirely and logs forwarded to your SIEM.
[07:22] Marco: Great. Now about model variants and quantization — Priya mentioned accuracy regression risk when switching quant. How do you recommend minimizing regressions during rollout?
[07:31] Lina (Product): We integrate eval suites into the rollout pipeline — before rollouts we run a battery of regression tests on your golden prompt set; if delta exceeds thresholds we block the rollout or route a percentage of traffic to the new variant. We also store per-prompt quality metrics in Console.
[07:47] Priya: Will those evals run under load? We care about perf/latency interactions with quantized variants.
[07:53] Lina: You can run simultaneous perf+quality benchmarks — the benchmark harness we share includes both latency and token-level quality deltas. We'll include your sample traffic in the 48-hour run.
[08:05] Marco: Ok, look at the artifact you shared earlier — the bench spreadsheet. Can we have a custom column for payload size distribution?
[08:12] Ben: Yes, please send sample histograms. Jonas, if you can drop the traffic CSV into the link, we'll import.
[08:18] Jonas: Will do. Expect that by EOD tomorrow.
[08:22] [08:22] Alice: Quick recap: Redwood will send pricing + Dedicated configs, SE will run the 48-hour benchmark with NexGen traffic pattern, security docs and KMS notes to be shared, and follow-up deep dive on private networking. Any other items?
[08:36] Priya: One more: how do you instrument client-side timeouts for observability? We want tracing across hops.
[08:43] Ben: We emit per-token and per-chunk traces that integrate with Jaeger/OTel. You can see end-to-end request traces in Console with span annotations for queueing, encode, decode, and network.
[08:58] Marco: This was helpful. Concern: we still need reassurance around p99 under 2k sustained and no regression during rollout. The benchmark will be decisive.
[09:09] Alice: Totally. We'll prioritize the benchmark and include variant/quantization permutations.
[09:12] Speaker 1: (soft) thanks everyone
[09:14] Ben: I'll post the runbook + sample config in the CRM deal thread and ping Jonas.
[09:19] Alice: Thanks all — we'll follow up with calendar invite for the Jan deep dive.
[09:24] Marco: Thanks, talk soon.
